item.title: YouTube Coming to Apple TV
item.description: YouTube, the Internet’s most popular source for originally created content, becomes available on Apple TV next month, Apple announced today. Beginning in mid-June, Apple TV customers will be able to wirelessly stream videos directly from YouTube to their widescreen TVs. “This is the first time users can easily browse, find and watch YouTube videos right from their living room couch, and it’s really, really fun,” said Steve Jobs, Apple’s CEO.

item.title: Mac OS X Tip of the Week: Open Wide
item.description: Did you know that Mac OS X offers a simple way to increase the width of a column in Column View? It does, and it couldn’t be simpler. Find out how to automatically expand a single column — or every Column View column at once — in the latest Tip of the Week.

item.title: iTunes Plus Brings Higher Quality DRM-free Tracks to the iTunes Store
item.description: Apple today launched iTunes Plus. The new option for iTunes customers features DRM-free music tracks that offer — for just $1.29 per song — high-quality 256 kbps AAC encoding for audio quality indistinguishable from the original recordings. iTunes Plus debuts with singles and albums from EMI’s digital catalog of outstanding recordings from artists such as Coldplay, The Rolling Stones, Norah Jones, Frank Sinatra, Joss Stone, Pink Floyd, John Coltrane, and Paul McCartney, a dozen of whose classic albums are now available on iTunes for the first time.

item.title: Free Educational Content Now Available from iTunes U on the iTunes Store
item.description: Apple announces iTunes U. A dedicated area within the iTunes Store, iTunes U features free content – course lectures, language lessons, lab demonstrations, sports highlights, and campus tours — from such leading universities as Stanford University, UC Berkeley, Duke University, and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. iTunes U, created in collaboration with colleges and universities, allows anyone with access to iTunes to easily extend learning, explore interests, learn more about a school and stay connected with an alma mater.

item.title: Audio Gear for Rich Media
item.description: If adding audio to your feature articles or photo essays sounds like an excellent idea, you’ll need to invest in some essential hardware, software, and accessories. What do you need? “Audio Gear for Rich Media,” the second in a series of articles on the audio’s new role in journalism, offers suggestions.

item.title: Karin Fong: Viva Las Vegas
item.description: When über-developer Steve Wynn set out to create some visual splash at his new Wynn Las Vegas, he hit the talent jackpot with Karin Fong and the entertainment and design firm Imaginary Forces.

item.title: Andy Earl: Capturing Controversy
item.description: Fresh out of college, Andy Earl scored his first real gig as a pro photographer when Malcolm McLaren, the manager of the Sex Pistols, asked him to shoot an album cover for the New Romantic pop band Bow Wow Wow. When an unexpected controversy ensued, it almost became his last gig, too.

item.title: Tip of the Week: See Your File’s Hidden Info
item.description: How big is that image? How many files nestle inside that folder? Mac OS X knows. And so can you. Learn how you can display information about the contents of folders, size of images, length of songs, etc. We reveal all in the Mac OS X Tip of the Week.

item.title: iWork@work Profiles
item.description: What do a busy wedding photographer, a historian with the National History Center, and a groundbreaking architect have in common? They all depend on iWork to help them create stunning presentations, stationery, proposals, websites, portfolios, and newsletters.

item.title: Bill Frakes: Photo Finish
item.description: They call the Kentucky Derby the most exciting two minutes in sports. For photographer Bill Frakes the old cliché still rings true, even after shooting the event for more than 20 years. To him, it’s the most exhilarating event of the year. It’s also his most complex — and important — assignment. That’s why Frakes counts Aperture among his most prized equipment. “Aperture is quite simply, in my opinion, the most powerful archival tool that a photographer can use.”
